extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students in philosophy of mathematics; historians of mathematics; mathematically-informed philosophers
extracted.subtask_description: A survey-style academic overview of themes, questions, and evaluative virtues relevant to the philosophy of mathematical practice (PMP), focusing on history, foundations, technology, and epistemic virtues of mathematical products such as proofs and theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance of history / history-informed practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical attention to historical mathematical practice (e.g., Lakatos’ Proofs and Refutations) as a source of evidence about how mathematics actually develops, including quasi-empirical methods, refutation by counterexample, and the tentative, fallible nature of mathematical knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical case studies to ask questions such as: How does mathematics grow? What counts as progress? How do discovery and justification interact? Examples: Lakatos’ reconstruction of Euler’s theorem, influence of Polya on heuristics. Anti-patterns: treating mathematics as a static a priori body and ignoring historical methodological variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundational adequacy and choice of axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation of set-theoretic foundationalism and competing frameworks (category theory, homotopy type theory) including the acceptability of particular axioms (Axiom of Choice, Continuum Hypothesis, Large Cardinal Axioms) and the rationale for adopting new axioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess foundations by both mathematical practice and philosophical rationale: whether a foundation plausibly accounts for current mathematics, how new axioms are motivated, and the interplay between philosophical motivation and technical development. See debates involving Woodin, Hamkins, Maddy, and work on HoTT (Voevodsky).

rubrics_metrics.name: Technological impact on proof epistemology
rubrics_metrics.description: How computational tools (computer-assisted proofs, interactive theorem provers (ITPs), and emerging AI tools) affect the nature, acceptability, and epistemic status of mathematical proofs and results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider issues of surveyability (can a single mathematician check the proof?), correctness, formalization, and the borderline epistemic status of computer-assisted proofs. Examples: Appel & Haken (4-color theorem), Hales’ Kepler proof and its formalization (Hales et al. 2017), Göthier’s formalization of the 4-color theorem, increasing use of ITPs (Avigad, Buzzard). Anti-patterns: automatically dismissing computer-assisted or formalized proofs without evaluating their formal verification or explanatory contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attitude toward foundationalism: ecumenical vs anti-foundationalist
rubrics_metrics.description: A meta-methodological stance about whether PMP complements foundationalist programs (ecumenical) or opposes them outright (anti-foundationalist), with consequences for what questions are prioritized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ecumenical view treats foundational work as valuable and complementary to practice-based studies (e.g., Mancosu volume); anti-foundationalist view (e.g., Corfield, Lakatos) treats foundationalist programs as inadequate and emphasizes practice, discovery, and historical methods. Evaluate authors and projects by which stance they adopt and the implications for research questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatoriness / mathematical explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a proof, theorem, or mathematical theory provides explanation (answers 'why') as opposed to merely establishing truth; explanatory virtue is highly valued and motivates alternative proofs and reformulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate proofs and theories for their explanatory power: do they make clear why a result holds? Examples from science: Baker’s cicada-prime-period example and Hales’ honeycomb (honeycomb conjecture) as cases where mathematics plays an essential explanatory role in empirical explanations. Within mathematics, prefer proofs that illuminate structure or uniformity (Brumfiel’s preference for non-transcendental proofs). Anti-patterns: treating a short or efficient proof as fully satisfactory when it gives no explanatory insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indispensability and ontological commitment via explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Enhanced indispensability criterion: if mathematics plays a genuinely explanatory role in our best scientific theories, this provides a reason to be ontologically committed to the mathematical entities involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing ontological commitments, consider whether the mathematical component is essential and genuinely explanatory (not merely descriptive) in scientific explanations. Use the structure of enhanced indispensability arguments (premises that mathematics is indispensable and that we should commit to entities posited by our best theories). Examples: Baker’s account, debates between Colyvan and Melia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity of methods (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: The virtue that proofs or solutions should use only conceptual resources appropriate to the disciplinary or topical content of the statement being proved (a cluster of related purity notions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess purity by asking whether the methods appeal to concepts 'foreign' to the theorem’s content; note the historical prestige of purity (e.g., Selberg's elementary proof of the prime number theorem). Purity relates to explanation, conservativity, and mathematical aesthetics. Anti-patterns: privileging impurity simply because methods are powerful, without considering the epistemic tradeoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical purity
rubrics_metrics.description: A form of purity requiring that a proof stay within the conceptual boundaries of a mathematical discipline (e.g., analysis vs geometry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Bolzano’s analytic proof of the intermediate value theorem (eschewing geometry); number-theoretic vs transcendental proofs of Jacobi’s four-square theorem. Use geographical purity to ask whether methods cross disciplinary boundaries unnecessarily; consider historical shifts in what counts as disciplinary boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topical purity
rubrics_metrics.description: A more fine-grained purity: proofs should use means suggested by the content of the theorem (e.g., plane projective theorems should not rely on spatial or metric concepts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert’s critique of Desargues’ theorem (proof used space when theorem belongs to planar geometry) illustrates topical purity. Evaluate whether using 'stronger' or 'foreign' notions is justified by explanatory or other epistemic gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elemental purity
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea that a proof is elementally pure if it only draws on what is more elementary than the theorem itself (where 'more elementary' can be cognitively or metaphysically cashed out).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use elemental purity to compare relative strength/complexity of methods; it raises epistemological and metaphysical questions about what counts as 'more elementary.' Examples and distinctions are discussed in Arana’s work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syntactic purity
rubrics_metrics.description: A notion of purity concerning the formal/syntactic resources used in a proof (mentioned as one variant among purity notions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Syntactic purity focuses on formal language and derivational resources; consider it when discussing proof-theoretic conservativity, translations between proofs, or when formal structure matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigor (process/product ambiguity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rigor as an epistemic virtue applied both to mathematical activity (process) and to mathematical products (proofs/theories), ensuring reliability and distinguishing genuine proofs from merely persuasive arguments, while being historically and technologically variable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate rigor with attention to historical change (what counted as rigorous evolves), technological constraints, and the possibility that excessive emphasis on one notion of rigor can obstruct progress. Consider cases (17th century) where relaxation of classical rigor aided development. Anti-patterns: conflating 'rigor' with a single timeless standard and ignoring methodological shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualizability
rubrics_metrics.description: The cognitive accessibility of mathematical reasoning via visual or spatial representations (diagrams, pictures) that support understanding and grasp of proofs and structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether visual representations genuinely aid understanding and whether they are compatible with rigor; visualizability is often complementary to rigor rather than opposed. Examples: work on Euclid’s diagrammatic reasoning (Manders, Netz).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for uniform/non-transcendental proofs as explanatory
rubrics_metrics.description: A criterion that favors proofs applying uniformly across a class of structures (non-transcendental) because they are seen as providing explanation rather than merely a proof in a special case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brumfiel’s methodological refusal to use the transfer principle (calling such proofs transcendental) illustrates valuing uniform proofs that apply to all real closed fields. Use this criterion when explanatory uniformity is an aim; anti-patterns: accepting proofs that only 'work' for special models without addressing generality or explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other epistemic virtues (depth, simplicity, parsimony, fruitfulness, beauty, generalizability, epistemic economy)
rubrics_metrics.description: A collection of additional virtues often appealed to in mathematical practice: depth, simplicity, ontological parsimony, epistemic economy, fruitfulness, beauty, generalizability, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These virtues function as evaluative criteria for proofs, theories, and concepts; their relative weight depends on context. Use them to supplement judgments about proofs/theories alongside purity, explanation, rigor, and visualizability. Examples/references provided (Morris 2024 and others).
